Parkinsonism worsens after an antiemetic

A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops increasing rigidity and difficulty initiating movement several days after starting metoclopramide for nausea. His levodopa schedule and adherence are unchanged, and there is no intercurrent infection. Which action of the new medication best explains this deterioration?

  1. Activation of striatal dopamine receptors
  2. Central dopamine D2 receptor antagonism
  3. Dopamine precursor supplementation
  4. Selective peripheral COMT inhibition
  5. Muscarinic receptor antagonism
Answer and explanation

Central dopamine D2 receptor antagonism

Central dopamine blockade can worsen parkinsonism and oppose dopaminergic treatment.

Option explanations

Central dopamine D2 receptor antagonism: Central dopamine blockade can worsen parkinsonism and oppose dopaminergic treatment.

Dopamine precursor supplementation: A dopamine precursor would generally improve motor symptoms.

Selective peripheral COMT inhibition: Peripheral COMT inhibition can prolong levodopa action.

Muscarinic receptor antagonism: Antimuscarinic drugs may reduce tremor rather than cause this mechanism.

Activation of striatal dopamine receptors: Dopamine receptor activation is opposite to metoclopramide's effect.
